addressed_problems.content: In the experiments, the quaternion advantage over real-valued models at extreme sparsity levels disappeared when an early stopping criterion based on minimum validation loss was applied. This sensitivity suggests that the relative performance of quaternion and real pruned networks depends critically on training hyperparameters, such as the stopping criterion and training duration. It remains an open question to systematically explore how different hyperparameter choices (e.g., learning rate, pruning schedule, re-training procedure) affect the sparsity–accuracy tradeoff for quaternion versus real models, and to determine whether quaternion advantages can be reliably recovered under early stopping or other regularization strategies.

For deeper architectures such as ResNet-18 and VGG-16, which require batch normalization layers, the quaternion advantage over real models was not observed at any sparsity level. The current implementation uses a component-wise quaternion batch normalization that treats each component independently, potentially breaking the structural relationships between quaternion components that are essential for the model's representational power. It is unresolved whether an efficient, numerically tractable quaternion batch normalization that preserves the quaternion structure (or an alternative normalization strategy) would restore the quaternion advantage when pruning deep models, or whether the depth of the architecture itself inherently negates the benefits of quaternion representations under pruning.

The study was limited to six model–architecture pairs on three image classification datasets (MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100). It is unclear whether the observed advantage of pruned quaternion networks over real pruned networks at extreme sparsity levels generalizes to other vision tasks (e.g., semantic segmentation, object detection), to other input modalities (e.g., audio, speech, multi-dimensional signals), or to a broader set of network architectures (e.g., transformers, recurrent networks). Establishing this generalization is necessary to determine the practical utility of sparse quaternion networks in resource-constrained deployment scenarios.

The mechanistic cause of the quaternion advantage at extreme sparsity remains an open empirical and theoretical question. The paper observes that pruned quaternion models outperform their real counterparts when only a small fraction of the original parameters remain, but does not determine whether this advantage arises from the weight correlations imposed by the Hamilton product, from a different effective capacity per parameter, or from interactions between the quaternion structure and the pruning dynamics. A theoretical understanding of this phenomenon, possibly through analysis of the quaternion weight matrix's structure and its effect on gradient flow or representation capacity under pruning, is needed to guide the design of future sparse quaternion models.

Modern deep neural networks often contain very large numbers of trainable parameters, which makes deployment on resource-constrained devices (edge phones, embedded systems) difficult because of limits on memory, computation and energy. Prior compression strategies include model pruning (structured and unstructured), low-rank factorization and knowledge distillation; pruning in particular can drastically reduce parameter counts and, when combined with re-training, also reduce training resource needs. However, pruning research has primarily focused on regimes where the pruned model remains close in size or performance to the original; at extreme sparsities (e.g., >90% of weights removed) accuracy typically degrades and behavior becomes unpredictable. Separately, higher-dimensional data embeddings such as complex numbers and quaternions offer an orthogonal route to parameter reduction (a quaternion representation can map four real neurons into one quaternion neuron and thus reduce raw weight counts by ≈75% under the usual construction). What is missing from the prior state of knowledge is a systematic understanding of how aggressive weight pruning interacts with quaternion-valued network representations: specifically, whether (a) the empirical phenomena seen for real-valued networks (such as the lottery ticket effect: that specific pruned subnetworks can be re-trained from the original initialization to reach original accuracy) hold for quaternion networks, and (b) whether, at extreme sparsity levels where real pruned models lose accuracy, converting to quaternion representations can preserve accuracy better than comparable real pruned models. Because prior work studied pruning and quaternion networks independently (and quaternion papers typically compared dense quaternion vs dense real models rather than pruned variants), there is no established answer to whether combining pruning with quaternion-valued architectures yields practical advantages for very resource-limited deployment; consequently practitioners lack guidance about when to prefer a sparse quaternion model over a sparse real model for multi-dimensional inputs such as color images.

nodes.content: In real-valued networks the lottery ticket hypothesis demonstrated that particular pruned subnetworks can be re-trained from the original initialization to recover original accuracy, enabling training-time resource savings and a conceptual understanding of sparse trainable representations. Quaternion neural networks reduce parameter counts by weight-sharing induced by the Hamilton product, but it was previously unknown whether the same phenomenon — existence of re-trainable sparse subnetworks that preserve accuracy when re-initialized with the original weights — applies to quaternion parameterizations. Without evidence that lottery tickets exist for quaternions, it is unclear whether iterative pruning plus re-training from initialization is a viable training-time compression strategy for quaternion models; lacking this, one cannot reliably use pruning to reduce training costs or to obtain small sparse quaternion models that retain the representational capacity of the dense quaternion network.

Prior literature had shown that quaternion parameterizations can reduce dense-model parameter counts (≈75% reduction under standard neuron-grouping) and that pruning can produce small sparse models that sometimes outperform small dense models; nevertheless, there was no empirical characterization of how quaternion parameterizations interact with aggressive unstructured pruning. The specific unresolved question is whether the structural weight-sharing of quaternions helps preserve accuracy when models are pruned to extreme sparsities where real-valued pruned models typically experience sharp accuracy degradation. Absent direct experimental comparison, practitioners cannot determine whether, for stringent model-size constraints (single-digit percent of original weights), converting to quaternion representations before pruning yields a measurable accuracy advantage over pruning in the real domain, nor can they quantify the magnitude of any such advantage for standard vision architectures and datasets.

While the broader experimental question is whether quaternion pruning gives advantages at extreme sparsity, an important edge case is highly overparameterized models that already achieve very high accuracy on simple tasks. It was unknown whether the quaternion advantage at high sparsity would persist for such models. If quaternion representations were to fail systematically on fully-connected architectures or high-accuracy regimes, that would limit their applicability. Therefore it was necessary to determine whether a failure case (real outperforming quaternion at all sparsities) arises from the architectural class (fully-connected vs convolutional) or from model overcapacity and near-saturation of performance; this distinction matters for deciding when to recommend quaternion pruning in practice.

Experimental outcomes of pruning plus re-training can depend sensitively on training protocols and stopping criteria. Prior comparisons between pruned real and pruned quaternion networks lacked an assessment of whether commonly used training heuristics, such as early stopping based on validation loss, change the relative performance of the two parameterizations. Without this check, any reported quaternion advantage at extreme sparsity could be an artifact of fixed-length training rather than a robust property; determining whether the advantage persists under early-stopping conditions used in standard baselines is necessary for practical recommendations about training pruned quaternion models.

Extending the quaternion-pruning comparison to modern deep architectures requires a practical quaternion batch-normalization implementation. The original quaternion batchnorm formulation is computationally intensive, so a component-wise approximation was used for tractability; however, it was unknown whether deeper architectures with batch normalization would preserve the quaternion advantage at high sparsity or whether the optimizer–normalization interaction would negate quaternion benefits. Because many production-scale models use batch normalization and are deep, clarifying whether quaternion pruning remains beneficial in that setting is essential to assess applicability to state-of-the-art architectures.

Prior comparisons between quaternion and real networks focused primarily on dense models or on parameter count parity for dense networks; a systematic head-to-head evaluation that applies a consistent iterative global-pruning methodology, identical training hyperparameters and re-training-from-initialization across both parameterizations was lacking. Without a standardized experimental pipeline, observed differences could stem from mismatched pruning schedules, inconsistent re-training procedures, or different initialization/optimizer settings rather than from intrinsic properties of quaternion vs real parameterizations. A reproducible methodology that fixes these variables is necessary to attribute observed accuracy differences to the parameterization and sparsity rather than to experimental confounds.

Pruned quaternion-valued networks, when pruned via global iterative magnitude pruning and then re-trained from the original initialization for the same number of epochs as the unpruned model, can match or exceed the accuracy of the corresponding unpruned quaternion model across the six architecture–dataset pairs tested (Lenet-300-100 on MNIST; Conv-2, Conv-4, Conv-6 on CIFAR-10; Conv-4, Conv-6 on CIFAR-100). This establishes that sparse trainable subnetworks (i.e., lottery tickets) exist in quaternion-weight parameterizations under the applied pruning and re-training protocol.

metadata.narrative: The conclusion that lottery tickets exist for quaternion networks is well-supported within the tested scope: the phenomenon is replicated across six architecture-dataset pairs (H1) using an established protocol (H2), providing strong evidence that the mechanism generalizes within the split-ReLU quaternion implementation. The main load-bearing risk is that the paper only tests one activation function (P1), so the conclusion's generalization to other quaternion activation functions is unsupported. The highlights fully underwrite the claim for the tested activation and protocol; no offsetting relationship exists between P1 and the highlights, as neither H1 nor H2 provides evidence about other activations. The residual risk on generalization to other activations is unprotected.

nodes.title: Lottery ticket hypothesis holds for quaternion networks

nodes.content: For the architecture–dataset pairs consisting of Lenet-300-100 on MNIST, Conv-2, Conv-4, Conv-6 on CIFAR-10, and Conv-4, Conv-6 on CIFAR-100, at very high pruning rates (approximately $10\%$ or fewer weights remaining relative to the original real unpruned model) the pruned quaternion implementation attains higher classification accuracy than the correspondingly pruned real-valued implementation of the same architecture. As an explicit quantitative example, for Conv-4 on CIFAR-10 at approximately $3.12\%$ of the original model's weights, the pruned quaternion network achieves about $75\%$ test accuracy while the pruned real network attains about $62\%$ test accuracy, i.e., a gap of more than $10$ percentage points. This pattern—quaternion exceeding real at extreme sparsities—was observed for all tested convolutional architectures (Conv-2, Conv-4, Conv-6 on CIFAR-10 and Conv-4, Conv-6 on CIFAR-100) except for the high-accuracy Lenet-300-100 fully-connected network on MNIST.

metadata.narrative: The claim that quaternion networks outperform real networks at extreme sparsity carries significant load-bearing uncertainty. The early stopping experiment (Conclusion 4) directly threatens the robustness: under a standard training heuristic, the advantage disappears (P2, high p2=0.6). No highlight offsets this specific failure mode, so the conclusion's validity is unprotected against this boundary condition. Additionally, the comparison at the same percentage of original R weights conflates absolute sparsity with relative sparsity (P3, p2=0.3), though this is a less severe risk because the practical framing (same absolute parameter budget) is valid for deployment decisions. The consistency across five architectures (H3) supports the claim's generality within the fixed-epoch regime but does not address the early stopping sensitivity. The dominant risk is from P2; the conclusion should be interpreted as restricted to the fixed-epoch training protocol without early stopping.

nodes.title: Quaternion networks outperform real networks at extreme sparsity for several architectures

nodes.content: For the fully-connected Lenet-300-100 model on MNIST, across the tested pruning schedule and re-training protocol the real-valued implementation outperforms the quaternion implementation at every level of sparsity that was explored. A follow-up experiment with a smaller fully-connected model (Lenet-12, a single hidden layer with 12 real neurons) on MNIST restored the general pattern (quaternion outperforming real at extreme sparsity), indicating that the divergence observed for Lenet-300-100 is associated with the particular model's very high baseline accuracy (≈98%) and overparameterization rather than being a generic property of fully-connected architectures.

metadata.narrative: The observation that Lenet-300-100 on MNIST is an exception (real outperforms quaternion at all sparsities) is well-documented in Fig. 4a. The paper's proposed causal explanation—that overparameterization and high baseline accuracy cause the reversal—has limited support: only one follow-up experiment (Lenet-12) is provided (P4, p2=0.5). The follow-up (H4) is a strength that provides partial evidence for the explanation, creating a partially offsetting relationship: H4 preempts the alternative hypothesis that all fully-connected networks reverse the trend, but it does not rule out other confounds such as layer count or hyperparameter interactions. The causal attribution remains the main weak point; the existence of the exception itself is solid.

nodes.title: Exception: Lenet-300-100 on MNIST where real outperforms quaternion at all sparsities

nodes.content: When training used an early-stopping criterion based on minimum validation loss with patience 10 (the same early-stopping policy used in the cited lottery-ticket baseline), the empirical advantage of quaternion implementations at high sparsities disappeared for all tested models; specifically, under early stopping the pruned quaternion networks did not outperform pruned real networks at any sparsity level in the examined experiments (for example, Conv-2 on CIFAR-10).

metadata.narrative: The claim that early stopping removes the quaternion advantage is supported by a direct experiment (H5), but the evidence is explicitly shown only for Conv-2 (P5, p2=0.4) and only for a single patience value of 10 (P6, p2=0.3). The paper asserts the pattern holds for all models, but the corresponding plots are not provided. H5 preempts the failure mode of ignoring boundary conditions entirely, but does not offset the specific risk that other models may not follow the same pattern or that different patience values could restore the advantage. The overall credibility is moderate: the phenomenon exists for Conv-2 under patience 10, but generalization to other models and stopping configurations is unprotected.

nodes.title: Early stopping removes quaternion advantage

nodes.content: For two deeper convolutional architectures (ResNet-18 and VGG-16) that require batch normalization, the real-valued implementations outperformed the quaternion-valued implementations at all tested sparsity levels under the employed quaternion batch normalization implementation (component-wise batch normalization, which applies standard batch normalization independently to each of the four quaternion components, rather than the original matrix-valued quaternion batch normalization that respects quaternion algebra). It remains unresolved whether this reversal of the pattern (quaternion outperforming real at extreme sparsity for smaller architectures such as Conv-2, Conv-4, Conv-6) is due to the depth of the networks, the batch-normalization algorithm used for quaternions, or an interaction of both factors.

metadata.narrative: The conclusion is narrowly stated for the component-wise batchnorm implementation and is well-evidenced by experiments on ResNet-18 and VGG-16. The primary load-bearing risk is that this implementation is an approximation that may cause the underperformance (P7, p2=0.7). The paper's explicit acknowledgment (H6) preempts overinterpretation by delineating the scope, but does not offset the risk that a proper quaternion batchnorm would reverse the result. The conclusion's applicability to genuine deep quaternion networks is therefore highly uncertain; the mechanistic cause remains unresolved. For the narrow claim about the tested implementation, the evidence is solid.

nodes.title: For deeper architectures with batch normalization (ResNet-18, VGG-16), real outperforms quaternion under tested batchnorm implementation

nodes.content: A reproducible experimental protocol was implemented and applied: for each of the six architecture–dataset pairs (Lenet-300-100 on MNIST; Conv-2 on CIFAR-10; Conv-4 on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100; Conv-6 on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100), the real and quaternion equivalents were constructed so they have the same number of real neurons; quaternion networks used one-fourth the number of quaternion neurons (and hence approximately one-fourth the raw weight count); pruning was performed with global unstructured magnitude pruning removing $20\%$ of remaining weights per iteration; biases were exempt; pruned models were re-trained from the original initialization for the same number of epochs as the unpruned baseline (40 epochs for Lenet-300-100, Conv-2, Conv-4; 60 epochs for Conv-6; batch size 60; optimizer Adam with learning rates 1.2e-3 for Lenet-300-100, 2e-4 for Conv-2, 3e-4 for Conv-4 and Conv-6); pruning continued until accuracy fell below $30\%$ for two successive iterations. The accuracy-vs-sparsity curves and concrete numerical comparisons across these six configurations are reported.

metadata.narrative: The methodological protocol is described in sufficient detail for reproducibility (H7). However, two design choices introduce uncertainty in the fairness of the comparison: the input channel construction (P8) uses grayscale rather than alternatives, and the hyperparameters are not tuned separately for quaternion models (P9). These premises threaten the claim that the comparison is fully systematic and fair across parameterizations. H7 supports the reproducibility aspect but does not offset the fairness risks. The protocol is reproducible and useful as a baseline, but the inherent fairness of the real-vs-quaternion comparison is partially compromised by these design choices.

nodes.title: Methodological contribution: systematic iterative global-pruning comparison between real and quaternion networks

nodes.content:
In the quaternion neural networks under consideration—where each quaternion neuron uses a split activation function applying ReLU independently to each of the four quaternion components—the existence of lottery tickets (subnetworks re-trainable from the original initialization to match or exceed unpruned accuracy) is established. Other activation functions common in the quaternion neural network literature include the quaternion ReLU (which respects the Hamilton product structure) and component-wise hyperbolic tangent. The claim of existence of lottery tickets is limited to the split-ReLU implementation; no experiments were conducted under these alternative activation functions.
      Arena et al., "Neural networks for quaternion-valued function approximation", 1994 (source of split activation)

metadata.failure_mode: If alternate activation functions (e.g., quaternion ReLU) do not admit lottery tickets, then the conclusion would be restricted to the specific split-ReLU implementation, not to "quaternion networks" broadly. The scope of the conclusion would narrow from a general claim about quaternion parameterizations to a claim about one particular instantiation. Since the paper's title and framing suggest generality, this narrowing would substantially reduce the practical significance of the finding.

refs.text: Arena et al., "Neural networks for quaternion-valued function approximation", 1994 (source of split activation)

metadata.weakness_reason: The activation function is a core architectural choice that can significantly affect the loss landscape and trainability of quaternion networks. Split ReLU treats each component piecewise-linearly, which may produce different gradient and sparsity patterns than quaternion-valued activations that couple components. The paper provides no argument or experiment to suggest that lottery tickets would persist under other activations; therefore the claim about "quaternion networks" as a general class is unsupported beyond the specific activation used. The field has multiple established activation functions, so this is not a minor detail but a potentially consequential design choice.

nodes.title: Quaternion activation function generalization

nodes.content: In the comparison between pruned real and pruned quaternion networks at extreme sparsity, the training protocol uses a fixed number of epochs (40 or 60). When the same pruning schedule is applied with an early stopping criterion based on minimum validation loss with patience 10—the same criterion used in the Frankle & Carbin (2019) lottery ticket baseline—the accuracy of the pruned quaternion networks no longer exceeds that of the pruned real networks for any tested model at any sparsity level. For Conv-2 on CIFAR-10 as a concrete example, the accuracy curves for the two implementations become essentially coincident across sparsity levels.

metadata.failure_mode: If the early stopping result is taken as undermining the advantage, the core claim of Conclusion 2—that pruned quaternion networks systematically outperform pruned real networks at extreme sparsity—is no longer supported for training protocols that incorporate early stopping. Since early stopping is a common regularization method, the practical relevance of the advantage is substantially limited. The conclusion would need to be narrowed to "under fixed-epoch training without early stopping" rather than the unqualified superiority claim. The paper's own Fig. 6 provides direct counterevidence to the general statement, requiring the conclusion to be heavily qualified.
metadata.weakness_reason: The early stopping criterion is a standard practice in neural network training and was used in the seminal lottery ticket paper that this work extends. Its effect of eliminating the quaternion advantage suggests that the fixed-epoch protocol may give quaternion networks an advantage only because the real network converges more slowly or overfits under those conditions. The paper does not analyze why early stopping removes the advantage (e.g., the real network may be under-trained with fixed epochs and catch up with more training; early stopping may prevent the quaternion network from achieving its potential advantage). Because the paper does not establish the mechanism, the conclusion about quaternion advantage is contingent on the specific training stopping rule, which is a fragile foundation for a general claim.

nodes.title: Early stopping removes quaternion advantage

nodes.content: The accuracy comparison between pruned real (R) and pruned quaternion (Q) networks uses the x-axis "percentage of weights remaining compared to the original real model". At the same numerical value on this axis, the Q network has been pruned to a lower fraction of its own original weights than the R network, because the unpruned Q network has only about 25% of the weights of the unpruned R network. For example, at 3.12% of the original R weights, the Q network retains 3.12÷25 = 12.5% of its own original weights, while the R network retains only 3.12% of its own original weights. Thus the two networks are at different relative sparsity depths relative to their own starting sizes.

metadata.failure_mode: If the advantage at extreme sparsity is fully explained by the fact that Q maintains a larger fraction of its original weights, then the conclusion that "quaternion networks outperform real networks at extreme sparsity" would be misleading: the comparison is not fair in terms of pruning intensity relative to each network's own capacity. The conclusion would reduce to the known fact that a network with more parameters (relative to its own architecture) outperforms one with fewer, which is trivial. The claimed advantage specific to quaternion representation would lose its empirical support.
metadata.weakness_reason: The x-axis choice conflates two effects: the absolute parameter count advantage from the quaternion compression (4× weight reduction in the dense model) and the effect of pruning per se. The observed accuracy gap could be largely or entirely driven by the fact that the Q network is operating at a less aggressive relative pruning depth. To isolate the effect of quaternion structure, one would need to compare Q and R at the same fraction of their own original weight counts (e.g., at 50% of each network's own weights), but the paper does not provide this alternative view. Without this control, it is impossible to attribute the advantage specifically to the quaternion parameterization rather than to the unequal relative pruning burden.

nodes.title: Unequal relative sparsity levels in comparison

nodes.content: For the Lenet-300-100 fully-connected network on MNIST, the real implementation outperforms the quaternion implementation at all sparsity levels, contrary to the pattern observed for several convolutional architectures (Conv-2, Conv-4, Conv-6 on CIFAR-10 and Conv-4, Conv-6 on CIFAR-100) where quaternion implementations outperform real at extreme sparsity. To investigate this exception, a single additional experiment was conducted on a custom fully-connected model (Lenet-12, one hidden layer of 12 real neurons) on MNIST. In this model, which achieves lower baseline accuracy than Lenet-300-100, the quaternion advantage at high sparsity reappears. No other variations in model size, accuracy, or architecture were tested to confirm whether overparameterization and high baseline accuracy are the causal factors.

metadata.failure_mode: If the true cause of the exception is not overparameterization but another confounded factor (e.g., the specific learning rate, the initialization scheme, or architectural depth), then the conclusion that "the divergence is associated with the particular model's very high baseline accuracy and overparameterization" would be incorrect. The follow-up Lenet-12 experiment would not diagnose the actual cause, and the paper's interpretation of the exception would be misleading, potentially causing misapplication of the main claim to models where it does not hold.
metadata.weakness_reason: Establishing that overparameterization (as opposed to other differences between Lenet-300-100 and the convolutional models, such as the number of layers, fully-connected vs. convolutional structure, or the specific hyperparameters used) causes the exception requires a systematic ablation: varying the size/accuracy of the fully-connected network while holding other factors fixed. A single datapoint from a drastically smaller model (12 vs. 300 neurons in the hidden layer) cannot distinguish whether the relevant factor is model size, baseline accuracy, layer count, or something else. The proposed explanation is plausible but not empirically established by the evidence provided.

nodes.title: Limited evidence for overparameterization explanation of exception

nodes.content: The observation that under early stopping (minimum validation loss, patience 10) the quaternion advantage disappears is explicitly demonstrated for one model (Conv-2 on CIFAR-10), where the accuracy curves for the two implementations become essentially coincident across sparsity levels. No plots or tables are presented for the other tested architectures (Conv-4, Conv-6, Lenet-300-100, Conv-4 on CIFAR-100, Conv-6 on CIFAR-100) to support the assertion that the quaternion advantage disappears under early stopping for all these models.

metadata.failure_mode: If other models do not exhibit the same disappearance of the quaternion advantage under early stopping, then Conclusion 4's claim that early stopping removes the advantage for "all tested models" would be false. The general conclusion that the quaternion advantage is sensitive to early stopping would be weakened, and the documented sensitivity for Conv-2 would not warrant a blanket statement. This would affect the interpretation of Conclusion 2's robustness analysis.
metadata.weakness_reason: The claim that the early stopping effect is universal across all tested models rests on a single visual demonstration. Without presenting the other models' results, the reader cannot assess whether the disappearance of the advantage is consistent across architectures or whether it varies in magnitude or even reverses. The lack of full disclosure raises the possibility that the effect is not uniform and that the claim is overgeneralized from a single example.

nodes.title: Early stopping evidence shown only for one model

nodes.content: The early stopping criterion used in the experiments is defined by a patience of 10 consecutive iterations without improvement in validation loss. No alternative patience values or other early stopping rules are tested. The sensitivity of the quaternion-versus-real comparison to the stopping criterion's configuration is not explored.

metadata.failure_mode: If with a different patience (e.g., 20) the quaternion advantage reappears, then Conclusion 4's claim is not robust: early stopping does not "remove" the advantage in general, only under one specific configuration. The conclusion would need to be qualified to the exact criterion used, reducing its scope and its relevance as a boundary condition for Conclusion 2.
metadata.weakness_reason: The patience parameter determines how much under-training or overfitting the model can undergo before stopping. A patience of 10 may be too restrictive for the pruned models, which might need more epochs to converge. If higher patience or alternative criteria restore the quaternion advantage, then the conclusion that early stopping generically removes the advantage would be incorrect. The paper does not show sensitivity to this parameter, leaving the robustness of the finding uncharacterized.

nodes.title: Patience parameter not explored for early stopping

nodes.content:
For the deeper architectures ResNet-18 and VGG-16, the quaternion implementation uses a component-wise batch normalization (standard batch normalization applied independently to each of the four quaternion components) instead of the original matrix-valued quaternion batch normalization that respects quaternion algebra. The original quaternion batch normalization is computationally intensive: adding a single batchnorm layer to Conv-2 increased training iteration time by approximately 40×. No experiment using the proper quaternion batch normalization is performed to determine whether the observed inferiority of the quaternion models (real outperforming quaternion at all sparsities) arises from the normalization approximation or from the network depth.
      Gaudet & Maida, "Deep Quaternion Networks", 2018 (original quaternion batchnorm)
      Yin et al., "Quaternion Convolutional Neural Network for Color Image Classification and Forensics", 2019 (component-wise batchnorm reference)

metadata.failure_mode: If the component-wise batchnorm is the cause of underperformance, then Conclusion 5 would not hold under a faithful quaternion batch normalization implementation: quaternion versions of ResNet-18 and VGG-16 might match or exceed real versions at extreme sparsity, following the pattern of the shallower architectures. The conclusion that "real outperforms quaternion" for deep architectures would be unsupported, and the paper's negative finding would be an artifact of the normalization technique rather than a meaningful architectural property.

refs.text: Gaudet & Maida, "Deep Quaternion Networks", 2018 (original quaternion batchnorm)
Yin et al., "Quaternion Convolutional Neural Network for Color Image Classification and Forensics", 2019 (component-wise batchnorm reference)

metadata.weakness_reason: Component-wise batchnorm breaks the quaternion structure by normalizing each component independently, potentially destroying the inter-component relationships that the Hamilton product is designed to capture. The paper acknowledges this limitation but does not characterize its effect. Without an ablation, the observed inferiority of Q cannot be attributed to the quaternion parameterization itself; it may be solely or largely an artifact of the normalization approximation. The practical constraint (40× slowdown) prevented the test, but this means the conclusion about deep architectures is inconclusive.

nodes.title: Component-wise batchnorm may cause quaternion underperformance

nodes.content: In the quaternion convolutional models for CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, the input image has three RGB channels. Because a quaternion neuron requires four input dimensions, a fourth channel is constructed from the grayscale (mean) values of the RGB channels. Alternative constructions exist (a constant zero channel, a replicated channel, or a learned channel through an additional trainable layer), and no tests are performed to compare their effects on the relative accuracy of real and quaternion models.

metadata.failure_mode: If the grayscale fourth channel puts the quaternion model at an advantage (or disadvantage) relative to using a zero channel or a learned channel, then the paper's comparative findings across all conclusions (2-5) that depend on the CIFAR experiments are contingent on this arbitrary input construction. The methodological protocol would not be comparable across different quaternion input encodings, limiting the reproducibility and generalization of the experimental pipeline.
metadata.weakness_reason: The input representation is the first layer of the network and can substantially affect what features are extracted. The grayscale addition mixes intensity information into the quaternion components, which may interact with the Hamilton product in ways that differ from other choices. Without testing alternatives, it is unclear whether the observed quaternion advantage (or lack thereof) is robust to this design choice or is an artifact of the particular input encoding. The choice could systematically favor either the real or quaternion model, introducing an uncontrolled confound.

nodes.title: Input channel construction for quaternion CIFAR models

nodes.content: The training hyperparameters (learning rate, optimizer, number of epochs) used for both real and quaternion implementations of each architecture are taken from the Frankle & Carbin (2019) baseline for real-valued models. No separate hyperparameter search is conducted for the quaternion models. The two parameterizations may have different optimal hyperparameter regions due to the different weight-sharing structure and loss landscape.

metadata.failure_mode: If the quaternion models would benefit from different learning rates or optimizers, the paper's comparisons (Conclusions 2-5) may not reflect the best achievable performance of quaternion networks under pruning. The conclusion that quaternion networks outperform at extreme sparsity could be an underestimate if Q hyperparameters could be improved, or an overestimate if the fixed hyperparameters happen to favor Q in certain regimes. The methodological claim of a fair comparison is undermined by the lack of separate hyperparameter tuning, as the comparison is not designed to find the best possible Q performance.
metadata.weakness_reason: Using identical hyperparameters assumes that both parameterizations share the same training dynamics, which is unlikely given the different architecture's weight-sharing structure. The paper provides no analysis of gradient statistics, learning rate sensitivity, or convergence patterns for the quaternion models. A well-tuned hyperparameter set for real models could be suboptimal for quaternion models, artificially suppressing their performance and making the comparison biased. The paper does not assess whether hyperparameter tuning could alter the conclusions (e.g., reducing the initial accuracy gap or changing the relative performance at extreme sparsity).

nodes.title: Same hyperparameters for real and quaternion models

nodes.content: The lottery ticket existence is tested on six distinct architecture–dataset pairs: Lenet-300-100 on MNIST, Conv-2 on CIFAR-10, Conv-4 on CIFAR-10, Conv-6 on CIFAR-10, Conv-4 on CIFAR-100, Conv-6 on CIFAR-100. In each case, the re-trained pruned quaternion network matches or exceeds the unpruned baseline accuracy at one or more sparsity levels.

metadata.credit: This breadth preempts the failure mode that the phenomenon is specific to a single architecture or dataset. Without this scope, a reader could dismiss the finding as a one-off result. The consistent pattern across all six pairs indicates that the lottery ticket phenomenon is a robust property of quaternion networks as implemented, providing confidence that the conclusion is not an artifact of a particular configuration. The credit is at the level of generalization scope: the conclusion is supported over a nontrivial range of architectures and tasks, not just a narrow point.

nodes.title: Systematic demonstration across six architecture-dataset pairs

nodes.content: The training and pruning procedure exactly follows the protocol of Frankle & Carbin (2019): iterative global magnitude pruning removing 20% of remaining weights per iteration, exemption of biases, re-training from the original initialization for the same number of epochs as the unpruned model, and averaging over 5 trials.

metadata.credit: This alignment means the conclusion can be directly interpreted within the established lottery ticket framework. The failure mode it preempts is that differences in protocol (e.g., pruning schedule, re-training procedure) could produce different results, making the quaternion finding incomparable to the real-valued baseline. By matching the protocol exactly, the paper shows that the difference is purely the quaternion parameterization, not procedural variation. The credit underwrites the causal attribution: the ticket existence is due to the quaternion structure under the standard procedure, not because of a divergent methodology.

refs.text: Frankle & Carbin, "The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis: Finding Sparse, Trainable Neural Networks", ICLR 2019

nodes.title: Faithful replication of known lottery ticket protocol

nodes.content: The quaternion advantage at high sparsity (curves for Q staying above curves for R below approximately 10% of original R weights) is observed for Conv-2 on CIFAR-10, Conv-4 on CIFAR-10, Conv-6 on CIFAR-10, Conv-4 on CIFAR-100, and Conv-6 on CIFAR-100 (five out of the six tested pairs, with the exception being Lenet-300-100 on MNIST).

metadata.credit: The consistency across five distinct architectures and two datasets preempts the failure mode that the finding is a single-dataset or single-architecture artifact. Without this breadth, the conclusion that "quaternion outperforms real at extreme sparsity" could be dismissed as a chance result. The pattern's occurrence across multiple independently varying conditions (convolutional depth, number of filters, dataset difficulty) suggests that the effect is a real consequence of the quaternion parameterization rather than a statistical fluke. The credit is at the level of generalization scope: the conclusion holds for a class of architectures (convolutional networks on visual classification), not just one specific case.

nodes.title: Consistent pattern across five convolutional architecture-dataset combinations

nodes.content: Having identified that Lenet-300-100 on MNIST violates the pattern (real outperforming quaternion at all sparsities), a custom fully-connected model (Lenet-12, single hidden layer with 12 real neurons) is tested on MNIST. This model achieves lower baseline accuracy than Lenet-300-100. In this follow-up experiment, the quaternion advantage at high sparsity reappears.

metadata.credit: This experiment provides a direct test of the hypothesis that overparameterization causes the exception. Without it, the exception would remain a potential counterexample that could limit the generality of the main finding. The follow-up isolates that fully-connected networks do not inherently lose the quaternion advantage; rather, the specific regime of near-perfect accuracy on a simple task does. This preempts the failure mode that the conclusion about quaternion advantage is invalid for all fully-connected models. The credit underwrites the interpretation of the exception: the paper offers a reasoned explanation supported by evidence, rather than merely noting an anomaly.

nodes.title: Follow-up experiment to probe the exception

nodes.content: The same experimental comparison is reproduced with an early stopping criterion (minimum validation loss, patience 10). Under this condition the quaternion advantage disappears: for Conv-2 on CIFAR-10, the accuracy curves for the real and quaternion implementations become essentially coincident across sparsity levels.

metadata.credit: This experiment addresses a clear boundary condition that could critically limit the practical applicability of the main conclusion. Without this check, a practitioner would be unaware that the quaternion advantage is fragile to a common training heuristic. The direct comparison with the fixed-epoch results provides evidence about the sensitivity, which is a strength of scientific thoroughness. The credit is in delimiting the scope of the conclusion: the paper proactively identifies a condition under which the advantage does not hold, allowing safer interpretation of the main claim.

nodes.title: Demonstrates a significant boundary condition for the main claim

nodes.content: The original quaternion batch normalization (Gaudet & Maida, 2018) is computationally intensive (adding a single batchnorm layer to Conv-2 increased training iteration time by approximately 40×), so a component-wise approximation (Yin et al., 2019) is used for the deeper architectures ResNet-18 and VGG-16. The paper explicitly states that whether the batchnorm layer or the network depth causes the reversal of the quaternion advantage is unclear and requires further investigation.

metadata.credit: This acknowledgment prevents the reader from overinterpreting the negative result. Without it, a reader might conclude that quaternion networks are fundamentally less effective for deep architectures. The paper specifies the caveat that the batchnorm approximation may compromise quaternion structure, leaving the mechanism unresolved. The credit is in scope discipline: the conclusion is explicitly bounded to the tested batchnorm implementation, and the paper does not overclaim general inferiority for deep quaternion networks. The failure mode of overgeneralization is directly preempted.

refs.text: Yin et al., "Quaternion Convolutional Neural Network for Color Image Classification and Forensics", 2019

nodes.title: Explicit acknowledgment of batchnorm approximation and its potential impact

nodes.content: Table 1 lists detailed architectures (number and type of layers, real and quaternion weight counts for all/conv layers), number of training epochs, batch size, optimizer, and learning rate for each model. The pruning schedule (global iterative, 20% per iteration, biases exempt, stop when accuracy drops below 30% for two iterations) is fully specified. The paper uses the public hTorch library (MIT License) for quaternion operations.

metadata.credit: This level of detail preempts the failure mode that the experiments cannot be reproduced or compared to future work. Without explicit architecture definitions and hyperparameters, the observed patterns would be difficult to verify or extend. The specification enables independent replication and systematic ablations, which is essential for a comparative methodology. The credit underwrites the credibility of the entire experimental pipeline: the observed accuracy differences can be attributed to the parameterization rather than to undocumented implementation choices.

nodes.title: Reproducible protocol description with architecture tables and hyperparameter details

steps.reasoning: Treat the methodological protocol as established knowledge: use the protocol described in conclusion 6 (construction of $\boldsymbol{R}$ and $\boldsymbol{Q}$ with equal numbers of real neurons, iterative global magnitude pruning removing $20\%$ per iteration, biases exempt, re-training pruned models from the original initialization for the same number of epochs, stopping when accuracy $<30\%$ for two successive iterations) as the experimental setup from which the empirical observation about trainable pruned quaternion subnetworks is derived.

Observe empirical behavior of pruned quaternion models under the above protocol: re-training pruned quaternion models from the original initialization for the same number of epochs as the unpruned model produced cases where the re-trained pruned quaternion model matched or exceeded the accuracy of the corresponding unpruned quaternion model; as a specific textual example, the paper states that "in Fig. 3a, a pruned model with $51\%$ weights ends training with higher accuracy than the unpruned model", and the paper asserts that "This result held for all six architecture-dataset pairs that we tested."
Fig. 3

Conclude existence of sparse trainable quaternion subnetworks: from the repeated empirical observation across all six architecture–dataset pairs that pruned quaternion models, when pruned and re-trained following the stated protocol, can match or exceed the original unpruned accuracy, conclude that sparse trainable subnetworks (i.e., lottery tickets) exist within the quaternion-weight parameterization under the applied pruning and re-training protocol.

Treat the methodological protocol as established knowledge: start from the experimental protocol summarized in conclusion 6 (construction of $\boldsymbol{R}$ and $\boldsymbol{Q}$ with equal numbers of real neurons, iterative global magnitude pruning removing $20\%$ per iteration, re-training pruned models from the original initialization for the same number of epochs, stopping when accuracy $<30\%$ for two successive iterations).

Examine the accuracy-vs-sparsity empirical curves for $\boldsymbol{R}$ and $\boldsymbol{Q}$: the paper reports aggregated accuracy-versus-sparsity plots for each architecture–dataset pair (the plots are presented as Fig. 4 for the six tested pairs). These curves show that $\boldsymbol{Q}$ curves begin at roughly $25\%$ remaining weights relative to $\boldsymbol{R}$ because unpruned $\boldsymbol{Q}$ have approximately one-fourth the number of parameters of $\boldsymbol{R}$ by construction; the region of interest is the high-pruning regime around $10\%$ remaining weights or lower.
Fig. 4

Describe the illustrative quantitative example from the Conv-4 on CIFAR-10 experiment: for Conv-4 on CIFAR-10 the paper describes that at about $12.5\%$ remaining weights the $\boldsymbol{R}$ and $\boldsymbol{Q}$ curves coincide, and on further pruning the $\boldsymbol{R}$ curve drops below the $\boldsymbol{Q}$ curve; specifically, at approximately $3.12\%$ remaining weights the reported test accuracies are close to $75\%$ for $\boldsymbol{Q}$ and about $62\%$ for $\boldsymbol{R}$, i.e., a gap of more than $10$ percentage points in favor of the quaternion implementation.
Fig. 4

Generalize the observed pattern across architectures: the paper states that this pattern—quaternion exceeding real at extreme sparsities (approximately $10\%$ or fewer weights remaining relative to the original real unpruned model)—was observed for all tested convolutional architectures in the study (Conv-2, Conv-4, Conv-6 on CIFAR-10 and Conv-4, Conv-6 on CIFAR-100), with the documented numerical example for Conv-4 on CIFAR-10 serving as an explicit illustration; note the one exception of Lenet-300-100 on MNIST which did not follow this pattern (addressed separately).
Fig. 4

Treat prior conclusions as given starting points: use conclusion 6 (the experimental protocol) and conclusion 2 (the general empirical pattern that quaternion models outperform real models at extreme sparsities for the tested convolutional architectures) as established empirical context for analyzing the Lenet-300-100 exception.

Report the anomalous empirical observation for Lenet-300-100 on MNIST: the accuracy-versus-sparsity plot for Lenet-300-100 on MNIST (presented as Fig. 4a in the paper) shows that across the pruning schedule and re-training protocol used, the real-valued implementation $\boldsymbol{R}$ outperforms the quaternion implementation $\boldsymbol{Q}$ at every level of sparsity explored; the paper explicitly states "For Lenet-300-100, however, $\boldsymbol{R}$ outperforms $\boldsymbol{Q}$ at every level of sparsity."
Fig. 4a

Conduct and report a follow-up experiment to probe the source of the anomaly: to determine whether the anomaly arises from the model being fully-connected or from other properties (e.g., very high baseline accuracy or overparameterization), the authors trained and pruned a smaller fully-connected model called Lenet-12 (defined as a model with a single hidden layer with 12 real neurons) on MNIST and ran the same pruning and re-training protocol; the pruning and training results for Lenet-12 are presented in Fig. 5, where the earlier pattern (quaternion outperforming real at extreme sparsity) reappears.
Fig. 5

Infer the most plausible explanation given the follow-up experiment: because Lenet-12 (also fully-connected) restored the general pattern while Lenet-300-100 did not, the divergence for Lenet-300-100 is attributed in the paper to properties of that particular model—namely its very high baseline test accuracy (reported as approximately $98\%$) and likely extreme overparameterization—rather than to the mere fact of being a fully-connected architecture. The authors assert this explanation as a plausible reason but do not derive it formally.

Record residual unexplained behavior as stated by the authors: the authors note that this explanation "cannot justify why $\boldsymbol{Q}$ underperforms $\boldsymbol{R}$ beyond the $4\%$ sparsity region for Lenet-300-100", i.e., they acknowledge that some aspects of the Lenet-300-100 divergence remain unexplained by the overparameterization hypothesis.
Treat the methodological protocol as established knowledge: use the protocol elements from conclusion 6 as the baseline experimental setup for the investigation of early-stopping effects.

Define the early-stopping policy used in the follow-up experiments: adopt an early-stopping criterion based on the minimum validation loss with a patience parameter of $10$ training epochs (i.e., stop training when validation loss has not decreased for $10$ consecutive epochs), which is the same early-stopping policy used in the cited lottery-ticket baseline.
[7]

Report the empirical effect of applying early stopping: when the experiments were repeated with the minimum-validation-loss early-stopping criterion with patience $10$, the empirical advantage of quaternion implementations at high sparsities disappeared for all tested models; specifically, under early stopping the pruned quaternion networks did not outperform pruned real networks at any sparsity level in the examined experiments. The paper provides the Conv-2 on CIFAR-10 example where the pruning results with early stopping are shown in Fig. 6 and should be compared with the earlier no-early-stopping result in Fig. 4b to see the disappearance of the quaternion advantage.
Fig. 6
Fig. 4b

Record the authors' implicit conclusion about training-time regime sensitivity: the authors present this observation as evidence that the observed quaternion advantage at extreme sparsities is sensitive to the training termination policy (i.e., whether full training for a fixed number of epochs is used versus an early-stopping policy); they report the empirical disappearance of the advantage but do not provide a mechanistic derivation of why early stopping removes the quaternion benefit.

Treat the methodological protocol as established knowledge: start from the experimental protocol described in conclusion 6 and note the extension to larger, deeper architectures which require batch normalization layers.

Describe the batch-normalization implementation choices and their contexts: the paper explains that an original quaternion batch-normalization algorithm treats a quaternion as a single entity and computes mean and variance using quaternion-valued matrix operations (this original method is referenced to prior work), but that implementation was prohibitively computationally expensive in practice (the paper reports that adding a single such quaternion batchnorm layer to Conv-2 increased the per-iteration training time by approximately $40\times$ relative to baseline). Therefore the authors used an alternative, faster implementation that applies batch normalization component-wise to each individual quaternion component (i.e., treat the four components separately), citing the alternative implementation in prior work.
[10]
[40]

Report empirical observations on the two deeper architectures: using the faster component-wise quaternion batchnorm implementation, the authors ran the pruning and re-training protocol on two deeper architectures, ResNet-18 and VGG-16, and observed that for both of these architectures the real-valued implementations $\boldsymbol{R}$ had greater accuracy than the quaternion implementations $\boldsymbol{Q}$ at all tested sparsity levels, i.e., the earlier trend where $\boldsymbol{Q}$ outperformed $\boldsymbol{R}$ at extreme sparsity reversed for these deeper models under the employed batchnorm implementation.

Record the unresolved causal attribution stated by the authors: the authors explicitly state that it remains unresolved from these experiments whether the reversal of the earlier trend is caused by the depth of the networks, by the component-wise batch-normalization algorithm used for quaternions, or by an interaction of both factors, and they identify this question as requiring further investigation.

State experimental goal and scope: the goal was to implement a reproducible experimental protocol to compare pruning behavior between real-valued networks and quaternion-valued networks across multiple architecture–dataset pairs, specifically the six combinations consisting of Lenet-300-100 on MNIST; Conv-2, Conv-4, Conv-6 on CIFAR-10; and Conv-4, Conv-6 on CIFAR-100, and to report accuracy-versus-sparsity curves for these comparisons. The architectures, datasets and hyper-parameters used are summarized in the table of experimental configurations referenced as Table 1 in the paper.
Table 1

Define the construction rule that made real and quaternion models comparable: denote $\boldsymbol{R}$ as the real-valued implementation and $\boldsymbol{Q}$ as the quaternion-valued implementation; require that both implementations have the same number of real neurons (i.e., the same dimensionality counted in real-valued neurons). Because one quaternion neuron corresponds to four real neurons, construct $\boldsymbol{Q}$ with one-fourth the number of quaternion neurons compared to the number of real neurons in $\boldsymbol{R}$, which implies approximately one-fourth the number of raw real-valued parameters in $\boldsymbol{Q}$ relative to $\boldsymbol{R}$ due to the weight-sharing property of the Hamilton product. The weight-reduction effect via quaternion representation is explained by the Hamilton product and the 4×4 real-matrix representation of a quaternion.
[29]
Fig. 1

Specify how input channels were handled and the exception for output layers: for grayscale inputs (MNIST), flatten the image and group every four pixels into one quaternion neuron; for RGB images (CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100), treat the RGB channels of each pixel as three components of a quaternion and add a fourth channel using the grayscale values of the input image as the additional channel; use a real-valued output layer for $\boldsymbol{Q}$ when the number of output labels (10) is not divisible by 4, so that the condition of equal numbers of real neurons across $\boldsymbol{R}$ and $\boldsymbol{Q}$ is maintained.
Table 1

Specify pruning algorithm and schedule: pruning was performed with global unstructured magnitude pruning where at each pruning iteration $20\%$ of the remaining weights (i.e., the $20\%$ of parameters with smallest absolute value across the entire model) are removed, biases are exempted from pruning, and pruning is applied iteratively. Define "pruned at iteration $t$" to mean that the surviving parameter set after $t$ successive $20\%$ global removals is used. Global pruning was chosen to be consistent with prior work showing it can find smaller lottery tickets in larger networks.
[7]

Specify re-training and stopping rules: after each pruning iteration the pruned model is re-trained from scratch using the original initial weights (that is, re-initialize the trainable parameters to the identical initialization that was used for the unpruned model) and trained for the same number of epochs as the unpruned baseline; continue iterative pruning until the model accuracy falls below $30\%$ for two successive pruning iterations, at which point pruning stops to conserve computational resources.
[7]
Table 1

List implementation and software details that form part of the reproducible protocol: experiments were implemented in PyTorch (the PyTorch library provided the base deep learning framework), quaternion operations and building blocks were constructed using the hTorch library, activations for quaternions used the split activation function that applies ReLU individually to each of the four quaternion components, quaternion back-propagation used the generalization of real/complex back-propagation, and all experiments ran on a single Nvidia RTX 3090 GPU.
[31]
[41]

State the data products produced by applying this protocol: the experiments produced accuracy-versus-sparsity curves for both $\boldsymbol{R}$ and $\boldsymbol{Q}$ for each architecture–dataset pair (the paper presents these as aggregated curves and reports means over five trials with standard-deviation error bars), enabling direct numerical comparisons across the six architecture–dataset configurations reported in Table 1.
Fig. 3
Fig. 4

open_questions.content: The experiments leave multiple scientific questions unresolved. First, it is unclear why quaternion advantages at extreme sparsity disappear when early stopping is applied; the sensitivity of the quaternion-versus-real sparsity tradeoff to stopping criteria and other training hyperparameters requires systematic exploration. Second, for deep architectures that require batch normalization, the current component-wise quaternion batchnorm is an approximation that may degrade quaternion structure; it remains open whether an efficient, numerically tractable quaternion batch-normalization implementation (or alternative normalization strategy) would restore the quaternion advantage for deep models such as ResNet-18 and VGG-16, or whether depth itself negates quaternion benefits under pruning. Third, the scope of tested tasks and architectures is limited (six model–dataset pairs in image classification); generalization to a broader set of vision tasks (e.g., semantic segmentation), other input modalities, and a wider model zoo has not been established. Finally, the mechanistic cause of the quaternion advantage at extreme sparsity — whether it arises from the Hamilton-product-imposed weight correlations, different effective capacity-per-weight, or interactions with pruning dynamics — remains an open empirical and theoretical question that the present study identifies but does not resolve.
